title: Doses and formulations
intro: A plain-language guide to the medicines used for gender-affirming hormone therapy in Australia: what each one is, what forms it comes in, the ranges Australian prescribers work within, and the blood tests that go with them. It is background reading, not a prescription.

sections.h: Start here: the dose is yours, and only your prescriber sets it
body: Every number on this page is a typical range that Australian prescribers work within. None of it is a recommendation for you.

Two people on the same medicine can be on very different doses and both be right. It depends on your goals, your blood results, your other health conditions, your age, and what your body does with the medicine.

Guidance is explicit that doses are individualised, and that some people — including many non-binary people — deliberately aim for partial effects on a lower dose. Low dose is not no dose, and it is a legitimate goal to raise with your prescriber [1][2].
list: Only a prescriber can set your dose, and only a prescriber should change it
Never start, stop, increase or skip a dose on your own
If your dose is not working for you, that is a conversation — not a change to make at home
Your pharmacist can talk it through with you for free, without an appointment
sections.note: If you are reading this to work out whether your own dose is right, the answer is not on this page. Take the question to your prescriber or your pharmacist.

body: Estradiol is the oestrogen used in feminising hormone therapy in Australia. It is the same hormone a body makes naturally, given as a medicine.
It comes as tablets, skin patches and skin gel. Which one suits you is a clinical decision, not just a preference.
Patches and gel avoid the first pass through the liver, so they are preferred where the risk of blood clots is higher [1].
Ethinylestradiol, the oestrogen in the combined pill, is not used for gender affirmation. The high doses used until 1989 were linked to more clots [1].

Estradiol injections and implants are not available as registered products here. Compounded versions exist, but they are not tested for potency, efficacy, safety or quality control, and Australian guidance advises caution [1].
list: Tablets — estradiol valerate (Progynova) or estradiol (Zumenon), commonly 2–8 mg daily, taken once a day or split into two doses [17]. Other guidance: the 2019 position statement gives 2–6 mg daily [1], and the Zumenon product information, written for menopause, uses one 2 mg tablet a day [29]
Tablets under the tongue — changes how the medicine is absorbed, so only do this if your prescriber has told you to [4]

Patches — Estradot or Estraderm MX, changed twice a week. Australian guidance gives a common range of 50–200 micrograms per 24 hours; many prescribers start low and build up every two to three months, which may mean wearing more than one patch at a time [17]

Gel — once daily, measured in pumps or sachets. Australian guidance gives one to four pumps of Estrogel (0.75 mg estradiol each) or one to two 1 g Sandrena sachets daily [17]. Other guidance: the Estrogel product information, written for menopause, says the long-term safety of more than two pumps a day has not been established [31]
Monitoring — oestradiol and total testosterone, rechecked six to eight weeks after any change [3]
sections.note: Estradiol tablets and patches are on the PBS with no restriction attached, so the usual co-payment applies. Both estradiol gels, Sandrena sachets and the Estrogel pump, are listed too [7][24].

body: These medicines lower the effect of testosterone. Oestrogen on its own does not usually suppress testosterone enough, so a blocker is often added.

Two are used in Australia: spironolactone and cyproterone acetate. There is no good head-to-head evidence that one is better than the other, so the choice comes down to your health history and how you tolerate it [1].

The advice is to use the lowest effective dose of cyproterone. The Australian product information reports meningioma with long-term use at doses of 25 mg a day and above, with the risk rising as the total dose taken over the years adds up. If a meningioma is diagnosed, cyproterone must be stopped permanently. Prolactinoma has also been reported [1][16].
After an orchidectomy a blocker is no longer needed. Oestrogen is usually paused around the time of surgery because of clot risk, so plan that with your surgeon and prescriber [1].
list: Spironolactone (Spiractin, Aldactone and generics) — a daily tablet, usually 50–200 mg daily in Australian guidance [17], and 100–200 mg in the 2019 position statement [1]
Spironolactone monitoring — it is also a diuretic, so blood tests check electrolytes and kidney function, along with your blood pressure [3]
Cyproterone acetate (Androcur, Anterone, Cyproterone Sandoz) — a stronger blocker, and a progestogen in its own right. Australian guidance gives 12.5 mg once a week up to 25 mg daily [17]
Cyproterone, lower still — 12.5 mg (a quarter tablet) every second day or twice a week is commonly used [17]
Cyproterone monitoring — blood tests usually include liver function [3]
Finasteride and dutasteride are not general blockers; they are commonly added for scalp hair loss, although Australian guidance notes it is unclear whether they add benefit [17]
sections.note: Spironolactone and potassium interact. Tell your pharmacist about any potassium supplements, salt substitutes or blood pressure medicines before you start.

body: A separate group of hormones that some people take alongside oestrogen. If one is used, Australia's 2026 standards of care prefer micronised progesterone (for example Prometrium) [17].
The evidence for whether progestogens add anything to breast development or mood is limited, which is why practice varies between prescribers. It is a reasonable thing to ask about.

They are also used the other way around. If periods continue on testosterone and cause distress, the options include raising the testosterone dose, an oral progestogen, or a progestogen-releasing IUD [1].
list: Micronised progesterone (Prometrium) — commonly 100–200 mg nightly, reviewed after three to six months [17]
No progesterone blood level target is given [17]

body: Testosterone is the medicine used in masculinising hormone therapy. In Australia it comes as a long-acting intramuscular injection, a daily gel, a daily cream, and shorter-acting injections [5].
The gels and cream suit a daily routine, or a dose adjusted in smaller steps. The long-acting injection is given by a clinician every few months.
Testosterone implants (pellets) are used by a small number of people. They last several months, but they are not PBS-subsidised and can only be made by a compounding pharmacy [5].
On the PBS, every testosterone product needs an Authority prescription. Your prescriber arranges that before you get to the pharmacy [6][10].
list: Testosterone undecanoate (Reandron 1000, and newer brands including Gonadron and Rejunon 1000) — 1,000 mg in 4 mL, deep intramuscular. A second dose about six weeks after the first, then one every 10 to 14 weeks [1][3][11]

Testosterone 1% gel (Testogel) — a metered pump delivering 12.5 mg per press, or 5 g sachets, applied daily. Australian standards give one to eight pumps, or one to two sachets, daily; four pumps is often enough for full masculinisation [17][10]
Testosterone 2% gel (Testavan), 23 mg per press, one to three presses daily, and 5% cream (AndroForte 5), 1–4 mL daily, often 2 mL [17][10]

Shorter-acting esters — testosterone enantate (Primoteston Depot) and Sustanon, usually 125–250 mg every two to four weeks [17]. Primoteston Depot was removed from the PBS on 1 February 2018 at the manufacturer's request and is now a private prescription [32]; Sustanon is not PBS-subsidised either [10][13]
Monitoring — trough total testosterone and haematocrit; see the blood tests section below [1][3]
sections.note: Testosterone can harm a developing pregnancy and does not reliably stop ovulation. If pregnancy is possible for you, contraception is worth a specific conversation with your prescriber — do not assume testosterone covers it [1].

body: These medicines pause puberty by switching off the signal from the brain that drives it. They are given as an implant or a depot injection, always under specialist care.

Australia's standards of care for children and adolescents name goserelin (Zoladex), leuprorelin (Lucrin, Eligard) and triptorelin (Diphereline), repeated every one to six months, depending on the product [30].

Since 1 October 2026, triptorelin 3.75 mg (Diphereline), a monthly injection, has been on the PBS with no restriction (item 9378N), but its listing carries a note that it "is not for use in gender dysphoria in minors" [25]. So, like goserelin and leuprorelin, which are PBS-listed only for other conditions, it is a private prescription for puberty suppression. SA Health's model of care (2023) notes that a young person who cannot get them through a hospital faces a cost of several thousand dollars a year [8].

Access to goserelin has been changing. The 3.6 mg implant was due to leave the PBS on 1 November 2026, with a free Zoladex Continuity Program to follow [9]. The sponsor has since told the TGA it will keep supplying the implant and extend PBS access, and goserelin is not on the PBS list of deletions for 1 November 2026 [26][27]. If this affects you or your child, ask your prescriber and your pharmacist well before the next dose is due.
Blood tests are not something you pass or fail. They tell your prescriber whether the dose is doing what you both want, and whether anything needs watching.

For feminising therapy, Australia's 2026 standards of care recommend keeping trough oestradiol above about 250 pmol/L, without a fixed upper limit, and total testosterone below 2 nmol/L for people who want full suppression [17]. The 2019 position statement suggested 250–600 pmol/L [1].

For masculinising therapy, the usual target is a trough total testosterone of about 10–20 nmol/L [17]. Other guidance: the 2019 position statement and the 2020 Australian GP guides suggest 10–15 nmol/L [1][3][13]; Australia's 2026 standards of care, which this site follows, give about 10–20 [17]. Testosterone also thickens the blood, so haematocrit is checked; above about 0.50 the dose or the interval is usually reviewed [1][3]. The product information for several testosterone injections now also warns about SGLT-2 inhibitors, medicines for diabetes, heart failure or kidney disease such as empagliflozin or dapagliflozin. Taken with testosterone, they have been linked to too many red blood cells, so the blood count is checked more closely [28]. This warning is not yet in every product information, so tell your prescriber if you take one, whatever form of testosterone you use [33].
Reviews cover more than levels: blood pressure, weight, smoking, and how you are going in yourself — mood, energy, sleep, and whether the changes match what you hoped for [1][2].

Screening follows the organs you have, not your gender and not your hormones [1][2]. If you have a cervix, screening is still due every five years, and collecting your own swab is an option that many people find far easier than a speculum examination [15]. The same logic applies to breast or chest tissue, and to prostate tissue, which genital surgery does not remove [2].
list: Feminising — oestradiol and total testosterone; electrolytes and kidney function if you take spironolactone; liver function if you take cyproterone [1][3]
Masculinising — total testosterone, and a full blood count for haematocrit; liver function and lipids as your prescriber decides [1][3]
Either therapy — blood pressure and weight at each review; glucose or HbA1c and lipids periodically, particularly if you have other risk factors [1][2]
Puberty blockers — bone health is monitored, because blockers pause the bone strengthening that puberty normally provides [1][2]
Before starting — baseline bloods, and a conversation about fertility and about contraception if pregnancy is possible, since neither testosterone nor oestrogen is reliable contraception [1][2]
Sexual health — STI and blood-borne virus testing as relevant to you, the same as for anyone [2]

Timing — review roughly every three months through the first year, then every six to twelve months, indefinitely [1][2]. Other guidance: Australia's 2026 standards of care suggest yearly reviews once things are stable [17]. After a change to oestrogen, levels are rechecked six to eight weeks later rather than straight away; after a change to the long-acting testosterone injection, the Equinox guide waits two more injections [3]
sections.note: Screening and monitoring are easy to lose track of when you move between services. Ask your GP to keep a written list of what is due and when, and ask for a copy yourself.

sections.h: Getting the timing of the blood test right
body: When the sample is taken matters as much as what is measured. Most targets in the guidelines are trough levels — the lowest point, just before the next dose is due [1][3].
A sample drawn at the wrong point can look far too high or too low when nothing is wrong, and lead to a dose change you did not need.

For Testogel or testosterone cream, your prescriber will usually want the sample in the morning before you apply that day's dose [3][17]. For Testavan, it is taken 2 to 4 hours after applying [17]. For the long-acting injection, the test is booked just before the next injection is due rather than soon after one.
sections.note: Ask for the required timing to be written on your pathology form, and tell the collection centre when your last dose was. It takes ten seconds and it saves repeat tests.

sections.h: If your medicine is hard to get
body: Shortages happen, and estradiol patches have been the long-running one. The 25, 50, 75 and 100 microgram Estradot patches are still in short supply, with the TGA estimating a return to normal supply by 31 December 2026; the [supply page](#/supply) shows the latest position [12].

The TGA has approved substitution for these patches, so where it is appropriate your pharmacist can supply a different brand or strength that delivers the same amount of estradiol per day, without a new prescription. That approval runs to 28 February 2027 [14].
Ask your pharmacist what is available and whether the product they can get is PBS-subsidised. Bring it up before you run out, not on your last day of supply.

International guidance is explicit that established hormone therapy should be continued rather than stopped, including through periods when your mental health is poor, unless there is a medical reason to stop [2]. Continuity is part of the treatment.

sections.h: Other medicines used alongside hormone therapy
body: Testosterone and oestrogen change more than the things someone is aiming for. Four effects come up often enough to have their own treatments: acne, scalp (androgenetic) hair loss, periods that keep coming despite testosterone, and vaginal dryness. Each is possible rather than certain — plenty of people never develop one or more of them — and the medicines used for them are ordinary prescriptions, not hormone therapy in a different form [3][17].

Acne on testosterone comes from the same mechanism as acne generally: androgens increase the size and output of the skin's oil (sebaceous) glands, and more oil means more breakouts on the face and body [5]. It tends to start within the first few weeks of treatment and is most active in the first one to two years, often settling after that even without treatment [13].

Australian guidance follows the usual escalation: a topical retinoid combined with benzoyl peroxide first, an oral tetracycline such as doxycycline if that is not enough, and isotretinoin — a stronger oral retinoid, usually managed with a dermatologist — for acne that is severe or scarring [13]. The three act at different points: the topical combination clears pores and reduces surface bacteria, doxycycline settles the inflammation that follows, and isotretinoin reduces the oil glands themselves, which is why it is kept for acne the other options have not controlled.

Testosterone is converted into dihydrotestosterone (DHT) by the enzyme 5-alpha reductase [23]. DHT drives most masculinising change, but its effect on hair follicles depends on where they sit: follicles on the beard, underarm and pubic area enlarge, while follicles at the temples, crown and front of the scalp tend to miniaturise — the same process behind male-pattern baldness [17]. It is slower to show than acne, typically taking over twelve months to become noticeable, and can continue for as long as testosterone does [17].

Topical minoxidil is a non-hormonal option; Australian product information is candid that exactly how it works is not known, though it appears to prolong the hair growth phase [22]. Finasteride instead blocks the enzyme that produces DHT in the scalp [23]. A small case review in trans men taking low-dose finasteride found modest improvement, without the sexual side effects reported in cisgender men on the same drug, though the evidence base remains limited [17]. It is contraindicated during pregnancy, relevant if a partner could become pregnant, and because it acts on the same pathway that drives masculinisation, some prescribers treat it as a trade-off to discuss rather than a routine add-on [17]. Hair loss can also take over a year to appear, so waiting before deciding on treatment is a reasonable choice [17].

Testosterone at gender-affirming doses does not reliably switch off ovulation, so periods can continue, especially in the first months of treatment [5]. On full-dose testosterone, periods are generally expected to stop within about six months, though this varies and not everyone reaches that point on testosterone alone; testosterone is not contraception regardless of whether periods have stopped [17].

If periods continue and cause distress, the options are reviewing whether the testosterone dose has reached target, an oral progestogen such as norethisterone or medroxyprogesterone acetate, or a levonorgestrel intrauterine device (IUD) [1]. Norethisterone is taken as tablets [18]; medroxyprogesterone acetate comes as tablets or as an injection given every three months [19]; the IUD is fitted once and can remain in place for several years [20]. The IUD and the three-monthly medroxyprogesterone injection also work as contraception; norethisterone and medroxyprogesterone tablets do not [17][18][19].

Testosterone suppresses the ovaries' own oestrogen production, and the vaginal lining depends on oestrogen to stay thick and lubricated. As that exposure drops, the tissue can thin and dry in a way similar to menopause, sometimes causing irritation, dryness or pain with penetration [5]. This tends to build up gradually over time on testosterone rather than appearing suddenly.

Low-dose vaginal oestrogen treats the tissue directly: daily for the first two weeks, then twice weekly, with product information describing systemic absorption as low enough that blood oestradiol stays within the usual postmenopausal range [21]. It acts locally and does not work against testosterone's effects elsewhere in the body [5]. Vaginal moisturisers, available without a prescription, are a non-hormonal alternative some people try first [17].
Each of these has its own page in the Medicines A–Z with doses, side effects and cost.
